title: Does foreign aid work?

turns.speaker: Ciara
turns.text: The budget's been cut again and the argument in the paper was the usual one. Decades of aid and nothing to show for it.

turns.speaker: Priti
turns.text: Which is wrong in a specific way. Health aid has an enormous record. Vaccination, malaria nets, the antiretroviral programmes.

turns.speaker: Yohan
turns.text: Those are the easy cases, though. Deliverable, measurable, technically simple.

turns.speaker: Priti
turns.text: They are, and they saved an extraordinary number of lives, so I'd rather not dismiss them as easy.

turns.speaker: Yohan
turns.text: Fair. My point is that the disappointing record is in the governance and institution-building part, which is most of the money.

turns.speaker: Ciara
turns.text: Because you're trying to build something from outside that only works if it's owned inside.

turns.speaker: Yohan
turns.text: Exactly. And a lot of it returns home anyway, through consultants and contractors from the donor country.

turns.speaker: Priti
turns.text: Tied aid, which has been criticised for forty years and hasn't gone away.

turns.speaker: Ciara
turns.text: The direct cash transfer evidence is the most interesting development, honestly. Give people money and they mostly use it sensibly.

turns.speaker: Yohan
turns.text: Which upsets everyone. Donors want a project with a photograph.

turns.speaker: Priti
turns.text: The other comparison nobody makes is against trade rules. Agricultural tariffs cost poorer countries more than aid gives them.

turns.speaker: Ciara
turns.text: So the same government takes with one hand and photographs the other.

points: Aid budgets are being cut on the argument that decades of aid achieved little.
Priti counters that health aid has a strong record in vaccination, malaria and antiretroviral programmes.
Yohan argues the disappointing record is in governance and institution-building, which absorbs most funding and cannot be built from outside.
Tied aid returns much spending to donor countries through consultants and contractors.
Direct cash transfers show good evidence but are unpopular with donors wanting visible projects.
Priti notes agricultural tariffs cost poorer countries more than aid provides, so donor governments take with one hand while giving with the other.
